newsitem.title: USA: Heston elected vice president of gun lobby group.
newsitem.headline: Heston elected vice president of gun lobby group.

text.p: Charlton Heston, the actor who played Moses and parted the Red Sea, has a new role -- helping to restore the reputation of the National Rifle Association.

The 72-year-old actor was elected first vice president on Monday by the 76-member NRA board, defeating incumbent Neal Knox, a hardliner who had led a challenge to oust executive vice president Wayne LaPierre.
Heston's narrow victory followed weeks of bitter infighting in the powerful gun lobby group as Knox sought to unseat LaPierre and steer the NRA in a different direction.
Speaking to reporters Monday, Heston said serving on the NRA board was one of the high points in his career.

"I never before had the chance to serve usefully on an organisation that defended the Bill of Rights," Heston said. "This is a sacred document in this country. It is unique to this country and I'm proud to be with an organisation that is devoted to protecting it."
Heston, who was also elected to the NRA board on Saturday, sought that seat in support of LaPierre, who was under fire for his handling of the group's finances.
LaPierre was re-elected, as was the group's president, Marion Hammer.
The board chose Kayne Robinson, assistant police chief in Des Moines, Iowa, as second vice president, ousting incumbent Albert Ross, who was also seen as a challenger to LaPierre's leadership.

Heston, a staunch Republican and a long-time member of the NRA, is widely expected to help repair the NRA's image, which has been tarnished by its opposition to the assault weapons ban and inflamatory comments by top NRA officials.
In 1995, former President George Bush resigned from the lobby group to protest a fund-raising letter written by LaPierre which described federal agents as government thugs.
The NRA later apologised for the remarks.
Since President Clinton's re-election last year, the NRA has scaled back its ambitions at least at the federal level, and no longer talks about repealing the ban on assault rifles as it once did.
But the group has been waging a state-by-state campaign aimed at expanding the right to carry a concealed weapon, now legal in 31 states.

In addition, a decision is expected from the Supreme Court soon in a lawsuit supported by the NRA that could weaken the federal Brady Bill requiring handgun registration. And the NRA this year was certified as a non-governmental organisation in the United Nations, where some member countries would like to see international handgun restrictions.
Heston, who made his theatrical debut as Santa Claus in a school play at age 5, became Hollywood's leading epic hero.
From Moses to Michelangelo, the Oscar-winning actor portrayed real-life luminaries with an integrity made all the more imposing by his muscular physique, rock-jawed face and resonant voice.
His craggy features and conservative lifestyle seemed to belong to another age.
A leader off screen and on, Heston served six terms as president of the Screen Actors Guild and was a chairman of the American Film Institute.
He is best known for his role as Moses in the 1956 epic "The 10 Commandments" in which he parted the Red Sea. In addition to playing Moses, Heston did the voice of God.
